hook.text: Bad data has crashed stock markets, exposed millions of records, and sent innocent people to jail.

buildup.text: Data disasters aren't random. They follow patterns: missing validation, unclear ownership, and silent failures.

discovery.text: Most disasters come from human error amplified by automation. Bad logic at scale causes damage at scale.

twist.text: The scariest disasters aren't the loud crashes. They're the quiet ones — wrong data trusted for months.

climax.text: Studying past failures is the fastest way to build systems that resist the same mistakes.

punchline.text: Learn from others' disasters. They're cheaper.

quiz.question: What causes most data disasters?
options: Human error amplified by automation at scale
Natural disasters destroying servers
Using open-source software

hook.text: In 45 minutes, Knight Capital lost $440 million. A software deployment gone wrong bankrupted a trading firm.

buildup.text: A technician forgot to deploy new code to one of eight servers. The old code activated a retired trading strategy.

discovery.text: The old code bought high and sold low — millions of times per minute — before anyone noticed.

twist.text: There were no automated checks to verify all servers ran the same version. One mismatch caused total ruin.

climax.text: Knight Capital was rescued by investors but lost its independence. All because of one missed deployment.

punchline.text: One server. One missed deploy. $440 million gone.

quiz.question: What caused Knight Capital's $440 million loss?
options: A missed code deployment on one of eight servers
A hacker breaking into their systems
A natural disaster taking servers offline

hook.text: NASA lost a $125 million Mars spacecraft because one team used metric units and the other used imperial.

buildup.text: The Mars Climate Orbiter was supposed to orbit Mars and study its atmosphere in 1999.

discovery.text: Lockheed Martin sent thrust data in pound-force seconds. NASA's software expected newton-seconds.

twist.text: The mismatch went undetected for months. The orbiter flew too close to Mars and disintegrated.

climax.text: A simple unit conversion error destroyed a mission. No data validation caught the mismatch.

punchline.text: Validate your units. Or lose your spacecraft.

quiz.question: What caused the Mars Climate Orbiter to fail?
options: A unit conversion mismatch between metric and imperial
A software virus
Insufficient fuel for the journey

hook.text: JPMorgan lost $6.2 billion because a risk spreadsheet had a formula error nobody caught.

buildup.text: In 2012, a trader nicknamed the London Whale built massive credit derivative positions.

discovery.text: The Value at Risk model was implemented in a spreadsheet that divided by a sum instead of an average.

twist.text: The error made risk look half as large as it really was. Management approved positions they would have rejected.

climax.text: A single formula error in one cell of one spreadsheet led to billions in losses and regulatory fines.

punchline.text: One wrong formula. Six billion dollars. Spreadsheets lie quietly.

quiz.question: What type of error caused JPMorgan's $6.2 billion London Whale loss?
options: A formula error in a risk calculation spreadsheet
A database server crash
An incorrect stock price feed

hook.text: On launch day, healthcare.gov could handle 1,100 users. Six million tried to log in.

buildup.text: The 2013 launch of the Affordable Care Act's website was a national embarrassment.

discovery.text: The site wasn't load-tested at scale. Data integrations with dozens of government agencies failed under pressure.

twist.text: The data problems ran deeper: identity verification services timed out, and enrollment data was lost or corrupted.

climax.text: A rescue team rebuilt the infrastructure in weeks. Load testing and data validation became non-negotiable.

punchline.text: Test at scale before launch. Not during.

quiz.question: What was a key technical failure of the healthcare.gov launch?
options: The system was never load-tested at the expected scale
The site used the wrong programming language
All data was stored in spreadsheets

hook.text: In 2017, hackers stole personal data of 147 million Americans from Equifax. Names, SSNs, birth dates — everything.

buildup.text: Equifax had a known vulnerability in their Apache Struts web framework. A patch existed but wasn't applied.

discovery.text: Attackers exploited the unpatched server for 76 days, extracting data from databases that lacked encryption.

twist.text: Equifax's breach detection systems had expired SSL certificates, so alerts weren't generated for months.

climax.text: The breach cost Equifax over $1.4 billion and led to the CEO's resignation. Patching is not optional.

punchline.text: One unpatched server. 147 million victims.

quiz.question: What allowed attackers to breach Equifax?
options: An unpatched known vulnerability in their web framework
A phishing email to the CEO
A physical break-in at a data center

hook.text: A quiz app harvested data from 87 million Facebook users. They never consented to political profiling.

buildup.text: Cambridge Analytica used Facebook's API to collect not just quiz-takers' data, but all their friends' data too.

discovery.text: The data was used to build psychological profiles for targeted political advertising in the 2016 election.

twist.text: Facebook's API policies allowed this data collection. The rules, not a hack, enabled the scandal.

climax.text: The fallout reshaped privacy regulations worldwide and led to Facebook's $5 billion FTC fine.

punchline.text: The data wasn't stolen. It was given away by design.

quiz.question: How did Cambridge Analytica obtain data from 87 million Facebook users?
options: Through Facebook's API, which allowed collecting friends' data
By hacking Facebook's servers
By purchasing data directly from Facebook

hook.text: Three billion accounts compromised. Every single Yahoo account. The largest data breach in history.

buildup.text: In 2013, attackers breached Yahoo and stole names, emails, phone numbers, and hashed passwords.

discovery.text: Yahoo didn't discover the breach until 2016 — three years later — during its acquisition by Verizon.

twist.text: The passwords were hashed with MD5, a broken algorithm. Attackers could crack most of them easily.

climax.text: Verizon lowered its acquisition price by $350 million. Late detection made a bad breach catastrophic.

punchline.text: Three billion accounts. Three years undetected.

quiz.question: How long did the Yahoo breach go undetected?
options: Approximately three years
Three days
Three months

hook.text: Hackers stole 40 million credit card numbers from Target during the 2013 holiday shopping season.

buildup.text: The attackers entered through a third-party HVAC vendor that had network access to Target's systems.

discovery.text: Malware on point-of-sale terminals captured card data in real time as customers swiped their cards.

twist.text: Target's security tools actually flagged the malware. The alerts were ignored by the security team.

climax.text: The breach cost Target $292 million and its CEO resigned. Third-party access became a top security concern.

punchline.text: The alert fired. Nobody listened.

quiz.question: How did attackers initially access Target's network?
options: Through a third-party HVAC vendor with network access
By guessing the admin password
Through an unpatched web application

hook.text: Every privacy breach follows a pattern: access too broad, detection too slow, response too late.

buildup.text: Common causes: unpatched software, excessive permissions, unencrypted data, and poor monitoring.

discovery.text: Prevention requires defense in depth: encryption, least-privilege access, patching, and active monitoring.

twist.text: Breaches can't always be prevented. But detection in hours instead of years dramatically limits damage.

climax.text: The companies that survive breaches are those that detect fast, respond transparently, and fix root causes.

punchline.text: You can't prevent every breach. You can detect it fast.

quiz.question: What is the most critical factor in limiting breach damage?
options: Speed of detection and response
Using the newest database
Having the largest security team

hook.text: Google predicted flu outbreaks from search queries. It worked brilliantly — until it didn't.

buildup.text: Google Flu Trends launched in 2008, predicting CDC flu data two weeks faster using search volume.

discovery.text: By 2013, it overestimated flu prevalence by 140%. The model confused media hype searches with actual illness.

twist.text: The model was never updated as search behavior changed. People's googling habits shifted but the model didn't.

climax.text: Google shut it down in 2015. Big data without domain knowledge and model maintenance leads to big mistakes.

punchline.text: Big data predicted flu. Until it predicted fear instead.

quiz.question: Why did Google Flu Trends fail?
options: It confused media-driven searches with actual flu cases
The CDC stopped sharing data
Google's servers were too slow

hook.text: A Harvard study said high debt kills economic growth. Governments cut spending based on it. The study had a bug.

buildup.text: Reinhart and Rogoff published a 2010 paper claiming GDP growth drops sharply when debt exceeds 90%.

discovery.text: A graduate student found that their Excel spreadsheet accidentally excluded five countries from the average.

twist.text: With the correct data, the growth decline was much smaller. Austerity policies were partly based on a coding error.

climax.text: The incident proved that peer review must include data and code review, not just the written paper.

punchline.text: One missed row in Excel. Austerity for millions.

quiz.question: What error did the Reinhart-Rogoff study contain?
options: An Excel formula excluded five countries from the calculation
They used fictional GDP data
The paper was written by AI

topics.title: Survivorship Bias in World War II

hook.text: The military wanted to armor the parts of planes that had the most bullet holes. A statistician said no.

buildup.text: Returning bombers had bullet holes in the fuselage and wings. The obvious fix: add armor there.

discovery.text: Abraham Wald realized the holes showed where planes could take damage and survive. The missing holes were fatal.

twist.text: The planes that didn't return were hit in engines and cockpits. The survivors were misleading the analysis.

climax.text: Survivorship bias means studying only successes — or survivors — and missing the critical failures.

punchline.text: The data you don't have matters more than the data you do.

quiz.question: What is survivorship bias?
options: Drawing conclusions only from survivors while ignoring failures
Having too much data to analyze
Data that expires over time

hook.text: Zillow used AI to buy homes at predicted prices. It lost $881 million and laid off 2,000 people.

buildup.text: Zillow Offers used machine learning to estimate home values and make instant purchase offers.

discovery.text: The model overestimated home values in volatile markets. Zillow bought thousands of homes above market price.

twist.text: The algorithm couldn't adapt to a cooling market fast enough. By the time data showed the shift, it had overpaid.

climax.text: Zillow shut down the program, proving that ML models need human oversight when stakes are measured in billions.

punchline.text: The algorithm was confident. The market disagreed.

quiz.question: Why did Zillow Offers fail?
options: The model overestimated home values in a changing market
Zillow ran out of storage space
Buyers refused to sell to Zillow

hook.text: Ice cream sales and drowning deaths are highly correlated. Should we ban ice cream?

buildup.text: Correlation measures how two variables move together. It says nothing about whether one causes the other.

discovery.text: Both ice cream and drowning increase in summer. The hidden variable — temperature — drives both.

twist.text: Data systems make it easy to find correlations at scale. Most of them are spurious and misleading.

climax.text: Acting on correlation without understanding causation leads to wrong decisions dressed up as data-driven.

punchline.text: Correlation is a clue, not a conclusion.

quiz.question: Why is acting on correlation alone dangerous?
options: Correlation doesn't prove that one variable causes the other
Correlations are always wrong
Only large datasets have correlations

hook.text: On February 28, 2017, a large chunk of the internet went down. The cause? A typo in an AWS command.

buildup.text: An Amazon engineer ran a debugging command that accidentally removed more S3 servers than intended.

discovery.text: Thousands of websites and services depending on S3 went offline, including Slack, Trello, and Quora.

twist.text: The outage revealed that half the internet quietly depended on one cloud region in Virginia.

climax.text: Amazon added safeguards: rate limits on server removals and mandatory confirmation for large-scale changes.

punchline.text: One typo. Half the internet. Gone for hours.

quiz.question: What caused the 2017 Amazon S3 outage?
options: An engineer's typo in a debugging command
A hacker attack on AWS
A power outage in the data center

hook.text: A tired GitLab engineer ran a database delete command on the production server instead of the staging one.

buildup.text: In 2017, during a late-night incident, a GitLab admin deleted the production PostgreSQL database.

discovery.text: Five backup methods were in place. None of them worked — they were either stale, misconfigured, or untested.

twist.text: The only working backup was a 6-hour-old staging snapshot. GitLab lost 6 hours of user data permanently.

climax.text: GitLab live-streamed the recovery and published a full post-mortem. Transparency turned disaster into trust.

punchline.text: Five backup methods. Zero that worked. Test your backups.

quiz.question: What lesson did the GitLab database deletion teach?
options: Backups must be regularly tested to confirm they work
Production databases should never have backups
Engineers should never work at night

hook.text: Cloudflare accidentally leaked sensitive user data into random web pages for months. They called it Cloudbleed.

buildup.text: In 2017, a bug in Cloudflare's HTML parser caused uninitialized memory to leak into HTTP responses.

discovery.text: Passwords, API keys, and private messages from millions of sites appeared in cached search results.

twist.text: Search engines cached the leaked data. Even after the fix, sensitive information was still findable on Google.

climax.text: Cloudflare worked with search engines to purge cached data and disclosed the bug within hours of discovery.

punchline.text: Memory leaks don't just crash programs. They expose secrets.

quiz.question: What was unusual about the Cloudbleed data leak?
options: Leaked data appeared in search engine caches
It only affected one website
It was caused by a physical hardware failure

hook.text: On October 4, 2021, Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp went offline for six hours. Globally.

buildup.text: A routine BGP configuration change accidentally withdrew Facebook's routes from the internet.

discovery.text: Without BGP routes, no DNS queries could reach Facebook's servers. The entire platform became unreachable.

twist.text: Engineers couldn't fix it remotely because their own internal tools ran on the same infrastructure.

climax.text: Someone had to physically enter a data center to reset the routers. Badge access systems were also down.

punchline.text: Facebook deleted itself from the internet. By accident.

quiz.question: Why couldn't Facebook engineers fix the outage remotely?
options: Their internal tools depended on the same infrastructure that failed
They didn't have the right passwords
It was a hardware problem at every data center

hook.text: In March 2021, an OVH data center in Strasbourg caught fire. Millions of websites vanished overnight.

buildup.text: OVH is one of Europe's largest cloud providers. The fire destroyed one building and damaged another.

discovery.text: Customers who relied solely on OVH's single-region storage lost data permanently. No off-site backups existed.

twist.text: OVH offered backup services, but many customers assumed their data was replicated. Assumptions aren't backups.

climax.text: The fire proved that cloud doesn't mean invincible. Physical disasters still destroy digital data.

punchline.text: The cloud is someone else's computer. And computers can burn.

quiz.question: What did the OVH fire reveal about cloud storage assumptions?
options: Cloud data is not automatically backed up across regions
Cloud providers never have fires
All cloud data is always replicated

hook.text: An AI hiring tool at Amazon penalized resumes containing the word 'women.' It learned bias from historical data.

buildup.text: The model was trained on 10 years of resumes. Since most hires were men, it learned to prefer male candidates.

discovery.text: Training data reflects the world as it was, including all its historical biases and inequalities.

twist.text: Amazon scrapped the tool, but the lesson remains: unbiased algorithms trained on biased data produce biased results.

climax.text: Auditing training data for representation and fairness is now a critical step before any model deployment.

punchline.text: The data was accurate. It was also deeply unfair.

quiz.question: Why did Amazon's AI hiring tool penalize female candidates?
options: It was trained on historical data that reflected gender imbalance
A programmer intentionally added the bias
The tool only processed male names

hook.text: A widely used healthcare algorithm gave white patients priority over sicker Black patients. It was trained on cost data.

buildup.text: The algorithm predicted which patients needed extra care. It used healthcare spending as a proxy for illness.

discovery.text: Black patients historically had less access to healthcare and therefore spent less — even when sicker.

twist.text: The algorithm wasn't explicitly racist. But using spending as a proxy for need encoded systemic inequality.

climax.text: Fixing the proxy — using actual health conditions instead of spending — reduced the bias by 84%.

punchline.text: The proxy was wrong. The consequences were real.

quiz.question: What caused racial bias in the healthcare algorithm?
options: Using spending as a proxy for illness, which reflected access inequality
Intentional racial discrimination in the code
Using too small a dataset

hook.text: A study found facial recognition misidentified dark-skinned women 35% of the time. Light-skinned men? Under 1%.

buildup.text: Facial recognition models were trained mostly on light-skinned faces, creating massive accuracy gaps.

discovery.text: MIT researcher Joy Buolamwini proved the disparity across Amazon, Microsoft, and IBM systems.

twist.text: These systems were already deployed by police. Wrongful arrests based on faulty matches had already occurred.

climax.text: The research led IBM to exit facial recognition and cities to ban police use of the technology.

punchline.text: If the training data isn't diverse, the model isn't fair.

quiz.question: Why did facial recognition systems perform poorly on dark-skinned women?
options: Training data was mostly composed of light-skinned faces
The cameras were broken
Dark-skinned faces have fewer features to detect

hook.text: Police send more officers to high-crime areas. More officers find more crime. The data says send even more.

buildup.text: Predictive policing uses historical crime data to forecast where crime will occur next.

discovery.text: The model doesn't predict crime. It predicts where police have previously made arrests.

twist.text: More policing in an area generates more arrest data, which trains the model to recommend more policing there.

climax.text: Feedback loops amplify existing biases. The algorithm doesn't create fairness — it automates the status quo.

punchline.text: The loop confirms its own bias. That's not prediction.

quiz.question: What is the feedback loop problem in predictive policing?
options: More policing generates more data that recommends even more policing
Officers ignore the predictions entirely
The algorithm only works in rural areas

hook.text: You built a model. It scores 95% accuracy. But for one demographic group, it's only 60%. Is it fair?

buildup.text: Bias auditing tests model performance across demographic groups: age, gender, race, and geography.

discovery.text: Fairness metrics include equal accuracy rates, equal false positive rates, and calibration across groups.

twist.text: There's no single definition of fairness. Different metrics can conflict — you can't satisfy them all at once.

climax.text: The goal isn't a perfect score. It's transparency about trade-offs and intentional choices about fairness.

punchline.text: Audit the model. Document the trade-offs. Decide openly.

quiz.question: Why is bias auditing challenging?
options: Different fairness metrics can conflict with each other
All models are equally fair
Auditing is too expensive to perform

hook.text: Google publishes detailed post-mortems for every major outage. The goal: make sure nobody repeats the mistake.

buildup.text: A post-mortem documents what happened, why it happened, what was done, and what will be changed.

discovery.text: Blameless post-mortems focus on systemic causes, not individual fault. People admit mistakes freely.

twist.text: Organizations that punish individuals for incidents get fewer incident reports — not fewer incidents.

climax.text: Post-mortems turn failures into institutional knowledge. Each disaster makes the next one less likely.

punchline.text: Blame the system, not the person. Then fix the system.

quiz.question: What is the key principle of a blameless post-mortem?
options: Focus on systemic causes rather than individual fault
Identify who made the mistake and penalize them
Only document what went right

hook.text: A castle doesn't rely on one wall. It has a moat, outer walls, inner walls, and a keep. Data systems need the same.

buildup.text: Defense in depth layers multiple safeguards so that no single failure causes a disaster.

discovery.text: Layers include access control, encryption, validation, monitoring, alerting, backups, and incident response.

twist.text: Every disaster in this course broke through because one layer was the only layer. Depth requires redundancy.

climax.text: No single safeguard is enough. The question is: when this one fails, what catches the problem next?

punchline.text: One wall falls. The next one holds. That's defense in depth.

quiz.question: What is the principle of defense in depth?
options: Layering multiple safeguards so no single failure causes disaster
Using the strongest possible single defense
Only defending the most valuable data

hook.text: Netflix intentionally kills its own servers in production. They call it Chaos Monkey. It makes them stronger.

buildup.text: Chaos engineering deliberately injects failures to test whether systems recover gracefully.

discovery.text: For data pipelines: what if a source table disappears? What if schema changes? What if a load spikes 10x?

twist.text: Most teams discover their pipeline's weaknesses from production incidents. Chaos testing finds them first.

climax.text: Controlled chaos in staging builds confidence that production will survive real chaos.

punchline.text: Break it on purpose. Fix it before it breaks for real.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of chaos engineering?
options: To discover system weaknesses by deliberately injecting failures
To destroy production systems permanently
To test user interface designs

hook.text: GDPR, CCPA, and SOX didn't appear from nowhere. Each was a response to data disasters that demanded change.

buildup.text: Enron's accounting fraud led to Sarbanes-Oxley. Equifax and Cambridge Analytica led to GDPR and CCPA.

discovery.text: Regulations force companies to implement controls they should have built voluntarily: auditing, consent, and deletion.

twist.text: Compliance isn't just legal overhead. The controls it mandates actually prevent the next disaster.

climax.text: Smart companies treat regulation as a floor, not a ceiling — exceeding requirements to build genuine trust.

punchline.text: Every regulation was once a disaster that could have been prevented.

quiz.question: What event directly contributed to the creation of GDPR?
options: High-profile data breaches and privacy scandals in Europe
A decline in cloud computing usage
The invention of blockchain

hook.text: Disasters will happen. The question isn't 'if' but 'how fast can you recover?'

buildup.text: Resilient systems combine prevention, detection, and recovery into a continuous cycle.

discovery.text: Key practices: tested backups, automated monitoring, runbooks, on-call rotations, and regular fire drills.

twist.text: The biggest resilience gains come from culture, not technology. Teams that practice recovery recover faster.

climax.text: Every disaster in this course was survivable with the right combination of preparation and rapid response.

punchline.text: You can't prevent every failure. But you can survive all of them.

quiz.question: What contributes most to building resilient data systems?
options: A culture of preparation, practice, and rapid response
Using only the newest technology
Having the largest engineering team possible
